articles.title: Two cargo ships sunk in Strait of Hormuz as Iran ramps up attacks in run-up to midterms
articles.summary: Two cargo ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being struck by unknown projectiles in separate incidents – highlighting the h...
articles.body:
Two cargo ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being struck by unknown projectiles in separate incidents – highlighting the heightened danger to shipping as Iran steps up attacks in an attempt to regain control over the critical waterway.

The Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride was struck on Tuesday while passing through the strait, catching fire and later sinking, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. All crew members were safely evacuated.

Videos verified by CNN show black smoke rising from the ship as it takes on water, while later footage and satellite images show cargo scattered in the water and a small oil slick. Iranian state media Press TV reported that the ship had "hit a sea mine on an unauthorized route" – which experts cast doubt on, saying a drone attack was more likely.

The merchant vessel Cape Dao, registered under Antigua and Barbuda, also sank, according to data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) on Wednesday – after it was first hit by projectile on September 23. One Indian crew member was killed.

While many vessels have been hit in the Strait of Hormuz this year, these are only the second and third to have sunk in the Middle East since the Iran war began in February, according to IMO data. Attacks have ramped up significantly since the end of September, once again reducing the amount of oil transiting out of the Middle East and raising oil prices around the world.

That's been a consistent headache for US President Donald Trump as the midterm elections approach, with gas prices, tariffs, and other factors driving up the cost of living top of mind for many voters.

Data from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) , which monitors shipping incidents, shows just how high the risk is. Nine attacks in or near the Strait of Hormuz have been reported since Monday, including a drone strike on a tanker.

Only 4.147 million barrels of oil successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday – less than a quarter of pre-war levels, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler. And the seven-day average of oil flow through Hormuz has dropped sharply since early October, Kpler's data shows.

"The sinking of Singapore-flagged GFS PRIDE marks a dangerous escalation after weeks of near-daily attacks on commercial shipping. Iran claims a naval mine; but a drone strike is more likely," said former US Navy officer Charlie Brown, also a senior adviser for United Against Nuclear Iran, a nonprofit that tracks and reports on Iranian sanctions violations.

"Many ask what response will the US Navy mount to Iran's escalating attacks on global shipping," he added. "But the real question is what response will other nations take? How long will the world tolerate this threat to shipping, seafarers and freedom of navigation?"

The US military continues to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports to maintain economic pressure on Iran. To some extent, it's worked: Iran's economy is in tatters, and in recent months it clearly lost its leverage over the strait, with the amount of oil flowing from other Gulf nations through the waterway increasing to near-normal levels .

That's partly thanks to a complex operation involving US-military-escorted "dark" transits across the strait at night, with tankers turning off their transponders to avoid detection.

That rise in oil flow is why Iran is now ramping up its attacks and threats, hoping to wrestle back the leverage it once had over the strait – especially as American voters head to the polls.

The Trump administration has tried to lower prices in other ways, including a controversial deal announced last week to drop some sanctions on Russia to import a relatively small amount of the country's diesel. But this has been met with bipartisan criticism – and there's no guarantee it will bring any substantial relief, with analysts warning that diesel could climb near all-time highs by November.

CNN's Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

articles.title: US teenager appears in court over alleged Hindu temple shooting plot
articles.summary: Alexandros Paporakis, 19, has appeared in court near Chicago after his arrest at the weekend.
articles.body:
A man has been arrested after an investigation into threats of a potential mass shooting that could have targeted a Hindu temple near Chicago.

Alexandros Paporakis, 19, from Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday. He was charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon for possessing a rifle with a barrel less than 16in long, the BBC's US partner CBS reports.

Police said they found a manifesto in which Paporakis identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people.

Prosecutors said the defendant told a colleague on the phone that his gun jammed and sent messages showing an AR-style rifle, CBS reports.

Other messages showed how the gun failed to fire when he pulled the trigger, and a photo of himself in a tactical vest, according to prosecutors.

This colleague and another coworker from the Taco Bell where Paporakis worked called police on Sunday to report the incident.

Palatine Police Chief William Nord said that officers "recovered a rifle, they recovered loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition, as well as body armour," while searching Paporakis' home.

Officers and the FBI were also able to examine Paporakis' electronics and electronic communications, where they said they found the manifesto.

"Reading through the manifesto, he did state some extremist ideologies and talked about violence, he talked about mass killings and how he wanted to carry out this mass shooting," Nord said, according to CBS.

Prosecutors allege that Paporakis' colleague told police the defendant had spoken about being a white supremacist while at work, and made disparaging comments about people of other races.

Prosecutors said that on Saturday, Paporakis told a worker he was planning "it" at a Hindu temple in Aurora, and said Sunday "was going to be a special day", before calling and sending the messages to his colleague the next day.

Police said that a specific intended location in the alleged threats has not been confirmed, and the investigation remains open.

Local Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi said he was "horrified" by the incident. In a statement posted on Facebook, he said: "Every American deserves to live and worship without fear, and we must stand together against hatred in all its forms."

articles.title: Washington building once occupied by the FBI is handed to a court-appointed receiver after months of missed payments on a $221.6 million loan
articles.summary: A historic building in downtown Washington, DC, that once housed a major FBI office has been handed to a court-appointed receiver after nine months of
articles.body: A historic building in downtown Washington, DC, that once housed a major FBI office has been handed to a court-appointed receiver after nine months of missed loan payments. The Woodies Building, located at 1025 F Street NW, came under the control of Trigild IVL following a court order issued on September 2, 2026. The property's outstanding loan balance has reached $221.6 million, up from the original $204.1 million borrowed in January 2017. The development follows the FBI's departure from approximately 200,000 square feet of office space. Although the building has secured new leasing deals involving Barnes & Noble, Netflix and Nvidia, the property is facing financial difficulties as its lender seeks to address the unpaid debt.The case followed a lawsuit filed by the lender's trustee, IGIS US Private Placement Real Estate Investment Trust No. 98, an investment trust associated with South Korean real estate manager IGIS Asset Management. According to a complaint filed on August 7, 2026, the borrowers stopped making monthly debt-service payments in December 2025. The lender also alleged that reserve payments had been missed since March 2025. The court appointed Trigild IVL to oversee the building's operations, finances and leasing following the dispute over the loan.FBI's departure left a major vacancy in the historic Washington buildingThe FBI's lease covering approximately 200,000 square feet was due to expire in November 2025. That space represented nearly 40% of the building's total area of roughly 500,000 square feet.A source with access to federal leasing records told Bisnow that the lease had been removed from the federal government's database by February 2026. The departure left a substantial amount of office space to be filled, affecting the building's potential rental income.Despite the FBI's departure, the Woodies Building has secured several prominent leasing arrangements.Barnes & Noble leased approximately 16,000 square feet of ground-floor retail space in 2025 and opened its bookstore in January 2026, bringing a retail presence to the historic property.Netflix signed a lease for approximately 19,000 square feet across the first and second floors in summer 2026. The space is intended for an office and entertainment hub.Nvidia secured a 27,600-square-foot sublease during the second quarter of 2026, according to Bisnow. Together, these arrangements cover approximately 62,600 square feet, substantially less than the area previously occupied by the FBI.A historic department store turned office and retail hubThe Woodies Building occupies an entire city block at 1025 F Street NW, directly above Washington's Metro Center station. The 10-storey property was the flagship location of Woodward & Lothrop, a prominent department-store chain that occupied the site from the early 1900s until the 1990s.After the department store closed, Douglas Development acquired and restored the building, converting it into an office and retail property. The redevelopment preserved distinctive architectural features, including intricate multicoloured engravings depicting figures from Greek mythology.Who owns the building?The borrowers named in the 2017 loan documents were Jemal's Cayre Woodies LLC and Jemal's Rich LLC, entities affiliated with Douglas Development Corp. Douglas Development founder and president Douglas Jemal and senior managing principal Norman Jemal were listed as borrowers.The lender's trustee sought the appointment of a receiver to take control of the property, and the court granted the request. Trigild IVL is now responsible for managing the building under the court order.Douglas Jemal, Norman Jemal and their attorney did not respond to Bisnow's requests for comment. The lender, its trustee and the receiver also did not respond to the outlet's requests.What happens to the Woodies Building next?Trigild IVL will oversee the building's finances, leasing and day-to-day operations while the loan dispute proceeds. The property could undergo a debt restructuring, a change in ownership or a foreclosure process, depending on how the dispute is resolved.The building's financial future will depend on the handling of its $221.6 million loan and its ability to generate rental income from existing and incoming tenants.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2005, George Lucas opened an 850,000-sq-ft digital arts campus on 23 acres of a former Army hospital in San Francisco; 21 years later, it has four buildings and a 17-acre public meadow
articles.summary: A giant bronze Yoda statue stands on a brick fountain in a quiet San Francisco park.
articles.body: A giant bronze Yoda statue stands on a brick fountain in a quiet San Francisco park. Behind it, four red-brick buildings house some of the world’s most advanced digital film studios. Rolling hills, streams, and old trees surround the site. In 2005, film director George Lucas opened this 850,000-square-foot digital arts campus on 23 acres of a former Army hospital site inside the Presidio of San Francisco. Two decades later, the Letterman Digital Arts Center has changed from a military medical site into a major creative hub. Here, classic park scenery meets modern film technology. The campus serves as the global headquarters for Lucasfilm, visual effects company Industrial Light & Magic, and game development teams. It brings together thousands of artists, programmers, and filmmakers on a site that remains open to the public.From military hospital to digital studioThe land where the campus now stands has a long history. According to historical records published by the Presidio Trust, the site was once home to the Letterman Army Medical Hospital, a large concrete building built in 1969. The hospital was named after Dr. Jonathan Letterman, who served as medical director for the Army of the Potomac during the American Civil War. When the Presidio military base closed in the 1990s, the land was transferred to the National Park Service and the Presidio Trust. Officials needed a lasting way to reuse the park’s military buildings and land. George Lucas won the right to redevelop the 23-acre site in 1999, beating several other commercial developers. An article in Wired magazine noted that Lucas proposed a low-rise design that would be kinder to the environment and fit the natural landscape of the historic park. His plan aimed to avoid blocking the area with tall office towers. Demolition of the old 10-story hospital began soon afterward. Construction crews crushed and recycled thousands of tons of concrete from the original building. They used the material to build the foundations and underground parking garages for the new campus. This recycling work helped the complex earn a LEED Gold rating from the U.S. Green Building Council. At the time, it was one of the largest environmentally certified commercial projects of its kind.A village built for creative artistsThe Letterman Digital Arts Center officially opened on 25 June 2005 with a private picnic for more than 2,000 staff members and guests. The total construction cost was about $350 million. The campus has four separate buildings designed in the classic Bay Area Craftsman style. They have dark red-brick walls, wide roof edges, and large windows that let in natural light. From the outside, the buildings look more like a historic university campus than a high-tech visual effects center. Inside, however, the campus has miles of fiber-optic cables, large computer servers, and modern screening rooms. Moving to the Presidio allowed Lucasfilm to bring its different divisions together under one roof. Before the move, teams worked at several locations in Marin County, including Skywalker Ranch and Big Rock Ranch. Moving Industrial Light & Magic to the Presidio brought computer animators, sound designers, physical prop makers, and company executives together so they could work more closely. The move brought around 1,500 jobs directly into San Francisco.Designed around a public parkOne of the main features of the Letterman Digital Arts Center is its focus on public space. Although the office interiors are secured to protect the secrecy of movie production, nearly 17 acres of the 23-acre property remain fully open to the public. Landscape architect Lawrence Halprin and his team designed the open grounds to blend with the surrounding national park. The grounds include green meadows, paved walking paths, a lagoon supplied with recycled water, and native plants that need little water. According to documentation from The Cultural Landscape Foundation, Halprin planned the park to offer views of the Golden Gate Bridge, San Francisco Bay, and the historic Palace of Fine Arts. The outdoor areas give visitors a quiet place to walk, eat lunch, or sit beside the stream. The park has few visible barriers, making the change from public parkland to private office space hard to notice.A steady destination for film fansThe public grounds have become a popular stop for tourists and local residents. The best-known spot is the entrance courtyard of Building B, where a life-sized bronze statue of Master Yoda stands on a stone fountain. Visitors often come to the courtyard to take photos with the statue. On weekdays, the main Lucasfilm lobby is open to the public. Inside, visitors can see life-sized statues of Darth Vader and Boba Fett, old movie props, and film awards. Even after The Walt Disney Company bought Lucasfilm in 2012, George Lucas kept personal ownership of the buildings. Lucasfilm and the other digital arts companies continue to rent their office space directly from Lucas under long-term leases. Over the past two decades, the campus has shown how an old urban site can be reused successfully. By replacing a concrete hospital with a digital arts campus set within a public park, the project kept open green spaces while giving the Bay Area film industry a permanent home.You use AI every day. articles.title: EC announces Special Summary Revision of voters' list in 17 states amid SIR row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission (EC) has informed the states that it would be conducting a Special Summary Revision of electoral rolls in 17 states,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission (EC) has informed the states that it would be conducting a Special Summary Revision of electoral rolls in 17 states, including the poll-bound states of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur and Goa.In a letter to the chief electoral officers of the states and Union territories concerned, including Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur and Goa, the Election Commission said January 1, 2027, would be the qualifying date for the exercise.The Special Summary Revision (SSR) is intended to add eligible voters, especially young people and first-time electors, rectify errors in existing entries and ensure electoral rolls are accurate and up to date.The current term of the 403-member Uttar Pradesh assembly ends on May 22 next year. The tenures of the assemblies in Manipur, Goa, Punjab and Uttarakhand, which have 60, 40, 117 and 70 seats, respectively, are due to end on different dates in March 2027.Under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, the Election Commission is permitted to conduct elections "earlier than six months before the term expires".Notice by ECHow's Special Revision different from SIRWhile a Summary Revision focuses on new eligibles and routine corrections, SIR goes far deeper, involving statewide house-to-house verification, detailed scrutiny of entries, and large-scale data audits.For instance, under a Summary Revision, a voter who has shifted homes must file a form to update their address. Under SIR, the Booth Level Officer visits that address, confirms whether the voter still lives there, checks if anyone new has become eligible, and updates the roll based on physical verification rather than waiting for the voter to initiate the change.The SIR of electoral rolls has triggered a political controversy, with opposition parties raising concerns over the deletion of voters' names and the possibility of eligible citizens being left out of electoral lists.The poll panel has maintained that the exercise is aimed at cleaning up electoral rolls by removing duplicate and ineligible entries, including those belonging to deceased voters, while ensuring that all eligible citizens are included.ALSO READ: ‘Anarchic, immature’: BJP targets Rahul over anti-CEC protests; claims misconduct with women copHowever, opposition parties have questioned the process, alleging that the exercise could lead to genuine voters losing their right to vote. They have also raised concerns over documentation requirements, verification procedures and the possibility of disproportionate effects on vulnerable groups, including migrant workers, the elderly and economically disadvantaged people.One of the main concerns surrounding SIR is the potential deletion of eligible voters' names during the verification process.The dispute has also reached the Supreme Court, with petitions raising concerns about the manner in which the revision is being conducted. The legal debate centres on the Election Commission's authority to revise electoral rolls and the safeguards available to voters who challenge their exclusion.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Amazon MGM Studios' Bray Studios plan should be approved - council
articles.summary: Amazon has used the studios since 2022 and bought it in 2024 but now wants to revamp the site.
articles.body:
Amazon MGM Studios' major revamp of Bray Film Studios should get the go-ahead next week, a council's planning officers have said.

The historic Water Oakley site was previously home to the iconic horror studio Hammer Films and used for the filming of movies including The Mummy and The Curse of Frankenstein.

Amazon has used the studios since 2022 and said its current proposals, which include building a multi-storey car park and six new sound stages, would help "realise the site's full potential".

The Royal Borough of Windsor and Maidenhead planning officers said the project should be given permission at a meeting on 22 October.

Listen to the latest news from Berkshire

The studios were also used for The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Alien, but the volume of production started to decline in the 1990s and 2000s and the site was nearly converted into housing.

In 2022, the Burke family, who previously owned the studios, got the go-ahead from the Royal Borough to revamp the site.

Two years later Amazon bought it to film some of its biggest shows. It has been used for the Lord of the Rings spin-off The Rings of Power and the second series of Citadel.

Plans for the redevelopment promise to bring forward a "world-class studio blending function and desirability" and Amazon wants to be able to film two productions at the same time there.

The plans include refurbishing the Grade II listed Down Place House and using it as a main production office.

A shuttle bus service is also proposed for production teams between the complex and Maidenhead, Windsor and Eton Riverside and Windsor and Eton Central train stations.

articles.title: A cash-strapped country, a persistent war machine: How Houthis are threatening MBS's Vision 2030
articles.summary: A missile does not need to destroy a skyline to threaten the future built around it.
articles.body: A missile does not need to destroy a skyline to threaten the future built around it. For Saudi Arabia, repeated Houthi attacks on airports and oil infrastructure have become more than a security threat. The recent strikes on Riyadh's airport have killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300, disrupted flights and affected major international events. They have also raised a larger question: Can one of the Middle East's wealthiest countries convince the world that it remains safe for business?That question is at the centre of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030. The ambitious plan seeks to reduce the kingdom's dependence on oil by attracting foreign investment, expanding tourism and turning Riyadh into a global business hub. Its success rests not only on grand projects and deep pockets, but also on the promise of stability. Investors, expatriates and tourists must believe that the risks are manageable.Yet the movement challenging that promise rules parts of a country where millions struggle to afford food. The Houthis have maintained a sophisticated missile and drone arsenal despite Yemen's economic collapse.How does a rebel group keep fighting, and can Saudi Arabia stop it without putting its own ambitions at risk?A hungry country with a long reachThe United Nations estimates that more than 22 million people in Yemen will need humanitarian assistance and protection in 2026. Some 18.3 million face acute food insecurity, while more than 2.2 million children under five are acutely malnourished.The Houthis control large parts of the country, including the capital, Sanaa, and have built a military capability that extends well beyond Yemen's borders. Their arsenal includes ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. Their forces have also threatened commercial shipping through the Red Sea, giving the movement influence over a vital trade route.The latest escalation has raised the stakes. After the Houthis seized strategic areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government. Saudi-backed forces have sought to recover territory, while the Houthis have retaliated with attacks on Saudi infrastructure.The movement's military reach rests on two foundations. It generates substantial revenue from territory under its control and uses overseas procurement networks to obtain the components needed for weapons production. Iranian assistance adds technology, training and expertise.The supply chainFor years, the image of Houthi weapons procurement was relatively straightforward: Iran supplied arms, smugglers moved them into Yemen, and the movement deployed them against its enemies. That remains part of the picture, but the network has become more complicated.The Wall Street Journal has reported that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps began supplying missile and drone components, alongside trainers, around 2015. Maritime interceptions subsequently made some established supply routes riskier. The Houthis responded by expanding their ability to assemble weapons locally, with help from Iranian specialists.This shift has made the movement less dependent on receiving complete weapons shipments. Instead, it can source individual components through commercial networks and combine them with locally assembled systems.Chinese-manufactured goods have become an important part of this picture. A study by Century International, cited by Alhurra, found that Chinese-origin materials accounted for around 35% of documented items identified in seized Houthi-bound shipments between 2021 and 2025, compared with 21% from Iran. It also found that dual-use items made up more than 80% of documented items in seized shipments in 2024 and 2025.Dual-use goods have legitimate civilian applications but can also be incorporated into military equipment. Electronics, industrial machinery, engines and specialist materials can therefore move through ordinary commercial channels before reaching a weapons workshop.A September report by Bloomberg described a July inspection that uncovered phenolic resin, a heat-resistant material used in missile construction, alongside tail fins resembling ballistic missile components. Other containers inspected in Aden contained items resembling missile bodies and guidance systems, as well as computer-controlled machine tools and drone-suitable engines.Conflict Armament Research has also documented components from Chinese suppliers in a Houthi missile related to Iran's Kheibar Shekan design.Why sanctions keep missing their targetThe growing use of commercial components presents a difficult problem for governments seeking to stop the flow of weapons. Sanctions can blacklist companies and individuals, while maritime interdictions can seize suspect cargo. Neither measure automatically dismantles a procurement network that can change suppliers, routes and intermediaries.Professor Harsh V Pant, vice-president at the Observer Research Foundation, said the central difficulty is that enforcement targets individual shipments and transactions, while Houthi procurement operates through a flexible network.Pant told TOI that "the supply chain has changed from weapons smuggling to distributed manufacturing".He said dual-use goods are difficult to distinguish from legitimate trade, while interdictions can simply push shipments towards alternative routes. Sanctions may increase costs without removing the ability to procure essential components.China's role creates a potential point of pressure. Its manufacturing base and export infrastructure provide access to a broad range of commercially available components, industrial equipment and logistics services. Pant argued that pressure on Chinese suppliers could constrain the Houthi weapons programme if it targets sensitive components, repeat procurement intermediaries and logistics firms.The objective, he said, should be to make replenishment slower, more expensive and less reliable over time, rather than assume sanctions can seal Yemen's borders.Sharma said domestic revenues from taxation, customs duties, fuel imports and control of commercial activity sustain the Houthi war effort, while Iranian assistance strengthens its missile and drone capabilities.“Targeted pressure on Chinese suppliers, combined with stronger export controls, financial monitoring and cooperation with Beijing, could restrict access to critical components. However, many of these goods have legitimate civilian uses, making enforcement difficult. Intelligence-sharing and coordinated international action are more likely to deliver lasting results than unilateral pressure or maritime interdictions alone.”Where does the money come from?Iranian assistance is important, but the Houthis do not depend entirely on Tehran to pay for their war effort. Much of their routine funding is raised in the territory they govern.Professor B L Shukla of Indira Gandhi National Tribal University said the movement draws revenue from taxes, customs duties, fuel imports and control over commercial activity. Iranian support provides military technology, components, training and expertise, strengthening the capabilities that domestic income helps sustain.The exact division between local funding and Iranian assistance is unclear. But Shukla said the distinction is important: domestic revenue keeps the system running, while external support enhances its military reach.A UN Panel of Experts on Yemen has documented the Houthis' control over customs, taxes, zakat and other sources of state income, alongside additional levies on economic activity. The Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington has estimated that around 70% of Yemen's tax revenue is collected in Houthi-controlled territory.Fuel is particularly valuable. The Houthis control the Red Sea ports of Hudaydah, Ras Isa and Al-Salif, through which a large share of Yemen's imports enter. Customs duties and the commercial fuel trade give the movement access to significant resources.The UN panel estimated that customs revenue from fuel imports generated around $4 billion between 2022 and 2024. Its findings also described the use of Houthi-linked companies and false country-of-origin certificates to circumvent sanctions.These revenues give the movement room to finance its administration, security apparatus and military activities. They also help explain why restricting Iranian weapons shipments alone may not be enough.Dr Ashok Sharma, Visiting Fellow at the University of New South Wales Canberra at the Australian Defence Force Academy, said the Houthis have built a relatively self-sustaining war economy, with domestic revenues keeping their operations running while Iranian assistance strengthens their weapons capabilities.“The Houthis generate substantial revenue through taxation, customs duties, fuel imports, smuggling and control of strategic ports. Iran remains crucial for advanced weapons technology, specialised components and training. Even a significant reduction in Iranian support may not dismantle the war machine, but it could weaken its technological sophistication and long-range strike capabilities.”A machine that feeds itselfThe different parts of the Houthi system reinforce one another. Control of territory provides income. Income helps fund procurement and weapons production. Missiles, drones and the threat of force strengthen the movement's military position, helping it maintain control over territory and revenue sources.The Houthis also use their military reach to pressure Riyadh politically. Threats to Saudi infrastructure raise the cost of backing the Yemeni government and increase the risks of a renewed war.The movement's influence over maritime traffic adds another lever. Its position near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives it the ability to threaten one of the key routes connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. That matters particularly now because Saudi Arabia has relied on its East-West pipeline to move oil towards Red Sea export terminals when disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has constrained other routes.This does not mean the Houthis can defeat Saudi Arabia in a conventional war. The kingdom has far greater financial resources and a much stronger air force. But the movement does not need to win a conventional battle to impose costs. It needs only to keep the threat credible and make the conflict expensive enough to test Riyadh's willingness to continue.The strategy carries serious consequences for Yemen itself. The renewed fighting has overwhelmed hospitals and cut off humanitarian assistance to hundreds of thousands of people, according to relief agencies. On October 14, Reuters reported that more than 200,000 people had been displaced in recent weeks as fighting intensified.A blurry visionFor years, Saudi Arabia has sought to replace its image as an oil-dependent state with that of an international business, tourism and investment hub. Vision 2030 is central to this effort.The attacks on Riyadh's airport have exposed the vulnerability of that promise. The subsequent strike on Aramco's headquarters has brought the threat closer to the infrastructure underpinning the kingdom's economy. Saudi authorities have said the company continued operating after the attack, but the episode has reinforced concerns about the security of critical facilities.The disruption is already visible in the events calendar. Reuters reported that several senior oil executives were removed from the schedule of the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh after the airport attacks. Saudi Arabia's flagship Future Investment Initiative, due later in October, faces the challenge of persuading international investors that the kingdom remains open for business.On October 15, the Gulf Cooperation Council announced that the EU-GCC summit, scheduled for October 24 in Riyadh, had been postponed. The GCC cited continued Houthi attacks and the suspension of flights at King Khalid International Airport as reasons for rescheduling the meeting.Saudi Arabia has maintained that it can withstand the disruption. Its energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, has stressed the kingdom's resilience, while organisers of major international conferences have sought to keep events on schedule with enhanced security arrangements.Pant said Saudi Arabia has significant financial and institutional buffers, including large foreign assets and strong capital reserves. These give the government the capacity to withstand shocks. But prolonged insecurity could undermine investment confidence and slow medium-term economic diversification.The IMF's July 2026 assessment reached a similar conclusion about the risks from the wider regional conflict. It said Saudi Arabia had shown resilience, but warned that a prolonged escalation could disrupt shipping, damage energy infrastructure and weaken investor confidence and diversification prospects.Pant cautioned that Saudi Arabia's reputation could become a larger long-term cost than the initial physical damage, although the two should not automatically be treated as competing priorities. The crucial issue is whether the state is seen as capable of protecting people and restoring normality quickly.Sharma said the reputational damage from repeated attacks could eventually outweigh the immediate physical destruction, as investors, tourists and skilled expatriates reassess the risks of operating in Saudi Arabia.“Missile attacks on Riyadh and critical infrastructure challenge the kingdom’s carefully cultivated image as a secure global business hub. Investors and expatriates can react within days through postponed visits, cancelled travel and tighter security measures. The real danger is sustained insecurity, which can gradually erode investor confidence and increase the cost of doing business.”MBS faces a difficult choiceFor Mohammed bin Salman, the stakes extend beyond international reputation. A substantial part of his domestic legitimacy rests on delivering economic diversification, employment opportunities and a higher standard of living. Vision 2030 is central to his promise that the kingdom can offer younger Saudis opportunities beyond the traditional oil economy.Persistent security threats could complicate that promise. A prolonged conflict may force the government to divert money and attention towards defence, while uncertainty could delay private investment and major projects.Shukla said investors may postpone decisions when risks rise, while expatriates could reconsider relocation if attacks become frequent. Sustained insecurity can also increase insurance costs and weaken confidence in Riyadh as a regional business hub.That leaves the crown prince facing three broad choices: intensify military action, pursue negotiations with the Houthis, or combine stronger defences with diplomatic engagement.A large-scale ground offensive could be costly and difficult to sustain. Yemen's mountainous terrain and divisions among anti-Houthi forces would make a decisive victory uncertain. The experience of Saudi Arabia's earlier intervention, which began in 2015 and was followed by a fragile UN-brokered truce in 2022, offers a warning against assuming military pressure will quickly resolve the conflict.Negotiations, meanwhile, would involve difficult compromises. The Houthis have previously sought concessions over revenue, salaries and their place in Yemen's political future. Riyadh would have to weigh the cost of compromise against the risks of an open-ended war.Shukla argued that the most sustainable approach would combine stronger air and missile defences, protection for critical infrastructure, efforts to disrupt illicit supply networks and diplomacy. Such a strategy would seek to reduce immediate threats without committing Saudi Arabia to another prolonged campaign.Sharma said Riyadh faces a choice between escalating its military campaign and pursuing negotiations, but argued that a combination of stronger defences, targeted pressure and diplomacy would better protect Vision 2030.“A large-scale military campaign could demonstrate resolve but risk drawing Saudi Arabia into another prolonged and expensive conflict. Negotiations without credible deterrence could encourage further Houthi attacks. A calibrated strategy combining stronger air and missile defences, disruption of weapons supply chains, diplomatic engagement with Iran and internationally supported negotiations offers a more sustainable path.”The real testSaudi Arabia has the resources to defend itself and cushion its economy against a period of instability. But resilience is not the same as immunity. Every new attack tests the kingdom's ability to protect its people, keep business moving and persuade investors that today's disruption will not become tomorrow's normality.The Houthis pose a difficult challenge because their strength does not depend on a single weapons shipment or an unlimited supply of Iranian cash. More airstrikes may damage facilities and raise the cost of fighting, but they cannot easily dismantle a system that adapts when individual routes are blocked.For Mohammed bin Salman, the choices carry risks on every side. Escalation could deepen the conflict, while negotiations may require painful compromises. The harder task is to contain the threat without allowing security spending and prolonged uncertainty to derail Vision 2030. The Houthis may never defeat Saudi Arabia on the battlefield. But by making the kingdom look unsafe, they can strike at the one target Mohammed bin Salman cannot afford to lose: confidence in the future he has promised.You use AI every day. The agreement includes a mutual assistance clause, largely linked to the presence of a significant French military base on Emirati territory.Abandoned by Washington?Since July 20, Saudi Arabia has also faced a maritime blockade imposed by Houthi militants. articles.title: Nigel Farage defends Reform's vetting after councillors filmed making racist comments
articles.summary: The Reform leader says "you can't vet for future comments", after undercover filming of party activists.
articles.body:
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.

Nigel Farage has insisted Reform UK does not have an issue with vetting, after ITV News broadcast undercover filming of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

The Reform leader told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments".

In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform , a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".

ITV's filming, gathered over a year, involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total.

Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.

Two years ago, Farage vowed to root out "bad apples" among Reform's candidates , saying "bigots" and "extremists" were not welcome.

Defending the party's vetting processes, Farage told BBC Look East: "You can't vet for future comments. You can look at someone's CV. You can look at someone's social media...

"I can't predict what they're going to say after a drink, when they're being provoked by somebody or egged on to say something."

Pressed over whether the party had an issue with vetting, he said: "No, not at all. We actually vet to a much higher standard than the other parties."

He insisted "appropriate action" would be taken following the broadcast, but added: "I'm promising you, however heavily you vet, you cannot stop what people say in the future."

ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.

These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, after defecting from the Conservative Party in 2025.

Feeney, Solihull's deputy mayor, told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites".

Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than 1% of British population can be non-white."

Farage said "the most egregious case" in ITV's filming was "somebody who is a long-term Conservative councillor", in an apparent reference to Feeney.

He said "anyone who says stuff like that" was "not welcome".

The Reform UK leader added: "But I promise you, if an undercover investigation spoke to hundreds of Labour councillors or Conservative councillors or however many hundreds they spoke to, and you provoke people, you'll find unsavoury things said by all parties."

Councillor suspended from prison job after 'despicable' comments

Bigots not welcome in Reform UK, says Nigel Farage

Reform candidate defects to Tories over racism row

On a different day in the ITV broadcast, Feeney is joined by two other Reform candidates, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, who discuss speculation of a mosque being built in the local area.

"There's got to be a way of stopping them - like, go and buy some pork chops; we'll bury it in the ground," Campbell is heard saying in the film.

Whelan says "we'll take pictures of it", prompting Feeney to add: "I was gonna say, 'Unfortunately, this is a pig cemetery, mate'."

Discussing a female Reform candidate from Birmingham, Feeney is heard saying, "I didn't know where to look", before Whelan adds: "I'd have been sniffing that seat as soon as she got up."

The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons" and would be continuing as an independent councillor.

The BBC has contacted Campbell and Whelan, who has resigned as a councillor, for a response.

A Reform UK Solihull spokesman condemned Feeney and Whelan's "misogynistic and offensive comments" and confirmed they were no longer Reform councillors.

The spokesman said Campbell's comment "was a joke in poor taste but with no malicious intent", adding: "It's something that he deeply regrets, and the party will not be taking any further action."

Elsewhere in the film, Dean Miller, a councillor in the south London borough of Bromley, is shown campaigning for Reform in the Makerfield by-election.

"We've been ethnically cleansed out of London because you never used to get any blacks over in Bromley," he tells an ITV undercover reporter. "And now, you know, Bromley's like massive Nigerian communities there."

Miller says he is "not racist", before later adding: "The Muslim thing, that is going to be that thing that takes over everything and then everyone just has one religion. Because, apparently, King Charles is a [expletive] Muslim... I think that's [expletive] traitorous."

ITV reported that Miller would now sit as an independent councillor having resigned from Reform and had told them in a statement that he was heavily medicated due to a chronic pain condition when he made the comments.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Reform should take "immediate and firm action against those who've been revealed to be making these abhorrent comments".

He added: "There is no place for any form of racism, antisemitism, discrimination in British politics, and we all should be relentless in repeating that and taking the firmest possible action."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "We should be asking why there's so many stories like this of people in Reform who are making these appalling comments."

Asked about one of the individuals being a former Tory councillor, she said: "It's not my problem anymore."

Badenoch added: "I don't want people like that in the Conservative Party. I'm glad they have gone."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."

A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

articles.title: 8-year-old Indian-origin girl dies of myocarditis after doctors missed warning signs; Australian coroner finds death preventable
articles.summary: A coroner has concluded that the preventable death of an 8-year-old Indian-origin girl in Australia was caused by medical negligence after doctors failed to recognize the severity of her myocarditis. The findings highlight significant lapses in care and oversight in the emergency department.
articles.body: An eight-year-old Indian-origin girl died from myocarditis at an Australian hospital in 2022 after a junior doctor failed to recognise the severity of her condition, a Victorian coroner has found, concluding that earlier medical intervention could have saved her life.Amrita Lanka died at Monash Medical Centre in Melbourne on April 30, 2022, less than 24 hours after arriving with vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain, according to ABC News.On Wednesday, Deputy State Coroner Paresa Spanos found that the care provided by overnight registrar Patrick Tan contributed to Amrita’s death. She said earlier escalation of treatment and a transfer to the Royal Children’s Hospital (RCH) could have saved her.“While I accept that EDs are busy places and Dr Tan was a relatively junior doctor with many responsibilities, the clinical management and care he provided to Amrita was wanting … and thereby caused or contributed to her death,” Spanos said.How did Amrita’s condition deteriorate?Amrita was referred to the hospital’s paediatric emergency department by her family doctor on April 29, 2022, after two days of illness. At triage shortly before 1pm, she was alert and her vital signs were within the normal range.Doctors initially suspected gastroenteritis, and she was placed in a cubicle without an allocated nurse.Later that night, her mother, Satya Tarapureddi, said Amrita began struggling to breathe. She told ABC News in 2022 that she pressed the staff assistance button but nobody came.“If they had paid more attention to her, maybe today my Amrita could be sitting next to me,” she said.Tan reviewed Amrita at about 3.20am on April 30. An electrocardiogram showed abnormal results, and he suspected myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart muscle. However, he told the inquest that he had not understood the severity of her condition.Tan said he was 12 weeks into his first paediatric rotation and responsible for about 18 patients during the overnight shift.Further blood tests were ordered, but Amrita did not receive proper attention again until about 5.30am. A troponin test, which measures heart muscle damage, returned a result exceeding 27,000 nanograms per litre, compared with a normal level below 10, the coroner said.Amrita was moved to the emergency department’s acute section, where she suffered three cardiac arrests. She died shortly after a retrieval team from the RCH arrived, as per the outlet.What did the coroner find?Spanos said several opportunities to intervene earlier had been missed. These included acting on high lactate levels and low blood pressure, which should have prompted a medical emergency call.She found that earlier escalation of care and transfer to the RCH, which provides specialist life-support services for children with critical heart and lung conditions, could have made the difference.By 8am, Amrita was receiving a high level of care from Monash doctors. However, Spanos said the opportunity to prevent her death had already passed.Two other doctors involved in Amrita’s treatment were cleared of responsibility.Hospital responseMonash Health conducted its own review in 2022 and acknowledged failings in the care provided before Amrita’s death. The health service has since changed its practices and policies and improved staff education, the coroner said.In a statement, Monash Health said it would carefully consider the findings.“Since Amrita’s death, Monash Health has made changes to strengthen patient monitoring, escalation of care and communication, and we remain committed to learning and improving patient safety,” it said.During the inquest, Spanos spoke about the loss felt by Amrita’s parents and brother. She described the girl as a talented child who loved art and animals, particularly birds, and played the piano.Her mother had previously described the possibility that better care might have saved her daughter as “torture”.You use AI every day. articles.title: Brazil plants 840,000 trees to restore 607 hectares of Atlantic Forest and reconnect wildlife habitats after 20 years of conservation
articles.summary: Brazil’s Atlantic Forest has lost much of its original cover after centuries of exploitation and deforestation.
articles.body: Brazil’s Atlantic Forest has lost much of its original cover after centuries of exploitation and deforestation. A conservation partnership between World Land Trust (WLT) and Brazilian NGO Reserva Ecológica de Guapiaçu (REGUA) has spent two decades protecting the remaining forest and restoring damaged habitats. REGUA has planted 840,000 trees on degraded land, restoring 607 hectares (1,500 acres) to forest.According to World Land Trust (WLT), the work has also created wildlife corridors between isolated forest fragments and helped reconnect populations of plants, animals and fungi. Alongside tree planting, REGUA has restored a lowland wetland where more than 220 bird species have been recorded.How wetland restoration brought wildlife back to the Atlantic ForestREGUA’s wetland restoration began in 2002 after the area had been converted to pasture and arable land in 1982. The original habitat consisted of swamp and flooded forest dominated by ‘Tabebuia cassinoides’ trees and tree ferns covered with bromeliads and orchids. Restoration involved building earth dams and diverting a small stream to create new lagoons.REGUA also reintroduced ‘Tabebuia’ trees and reforested the surrounding land. Over the following two decades, aquatic wildlife returned, including broad-snouted caiman, capybara, crakes, herons and wildfowl. More than 220 bird species have been recorded in the restored wetland. The habitat also proved suitable for reintroducing lowland tapir, marking the species’ return to Rio de Janeiro state after more than a century.How REGUA has restored 607 hectares of Brazil’s Atlantic ForestThe Atlantic Forest once covered 150 million hectares (371 million acres) across South America. However, centuries of exploitation and deforestation have reduced its original cover to a small fraction. A 2009 study estimated that just 11.7% remained, while other estimates put the figure as low as 7%. Around 83% of the surviving forest consists of isolated secondary forest fragments smaller than 50 hectares (124 acres).These patches cannot sustain viable populations of many species, particularly those unable to cross the gaps between them. REGUA was established in 2001 to protect the forest and biodiversity of the Guapiaçu watershed in the Serra dos Órgãos mountains of south-east Brazil. It has worked with WLT since 2005 to expand protection and restore degraded land.REGUA expanded its Atlantic Forest reserve to protect nearly 15,000 hectaresProtecting the remaining Atlantic Forest in the Guapiaçu watershed is a priority for REGUA. Expanding the reserve through land purchases helps secure habitats over the long term. In 2006, WLT funded one of REGUA’s earliest purchases, adding 259 hectares (641 acres) of protected forest. Donations from organisations and individuals have since enabled REGUA to add 10,139 hectares (25,053 acres) to the reserve.Over the past two decades, WLT has funded or part-funded 1,532 hectares (3,786 acres) of the land added to the reserve. REGUA also manages another 4,202 hectares (10,384 acres) through land management agreements and leases 652 hectares (1,611 acres). Together, these areas bring the total Atlantic Forest protected by REGUA to 14,993 hectares (37,048 acres), including degraded pasture and scrubland.REGUA grows thousands of trees to rebuild damaged habitatsREGUA has planted 840,000 trees on degraded land, mostly on purchased pasture, restoring 607 hectares (1,500 acres) to forest. The restored areas also form wildlife corridors between previously isolated forest fragments, helping reconnect genetically separated populations of flora, fauna and funga.REGUA established its tree nursery in 2005, and it now produces around 60,000 saplings annually. Most grow from seeds collected in the forest by the reserve’s rangers. The nursery raises up to 180 tree species, including pioneer and climax species, to increase diversity and begin ecological succession in replanted forests. Staff nurture seedlings until they are mature enough to have a better chance of survival. Planting takes place during summer, when regular seasonal rains help sustain young trees.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2013, childhood friends Peter Rahal and Jared Smith each put $5,000 into RXBAR and made bars in Rahal’s parents’ basement; four years later Kellogg bought the company for about $600 million
articles.summary: In 2013, two childhood friends from Glen Ellyn, Illinois, pooled $10,000 to buy egg whites, dates, and nuts.
articles.body: In 2013, two childhood friends from Glen Ellyn, Illinois, pooled $10,000 to buy egg whites, dates, and nuts. They made their first batch of protein bars in a suburban basement using a food processor. Four years later, global food company Kellogg Company bought their business for $600 million. Peter Rahal and Jared Smith founded Chicago Bar Company LLC, the Chicago-based company behind RXBAR, after growing tired of the long lists of artificial ingredients in regular protein snacks. With no outside investors, corporate office, or formal business experience, the pair built one of North America's fastest-growing natural food brands. The sale in October 2017 gave the founders a huge financial return and made RXBAR a major success story in the health food industry.Starting out in a family basementThe business began with a simple problem. Rahal and Smith had been close friends since primary school. Both were active CrossFit athletes who regularly ate protein bars. However, they struggled to find products made with simple, whole food ingredients and no added sugar or artificial additives. In early 2013, the pair decided to make their own alternative. Each put in $5,000 from personal savings to buy ingredients in bulk and basic kitchen tools. They set up their workspace in the basement of Rahal's parents' home in Glen Ellyn. After testing different recipes, they settled on a formula made with egg white protein, dates, and nuts. During the early months, the business relied entirely on direct sales to customers. Rahal and Smith mixed the ingredients by hand, packed the finished bars in wrappers designed using Microsoft PowerPoint, and sold them directly to local CrossFit gym owners and members across the Midwest. Their first plan focused on small fitness communities. The founders collected feedback directly from gym members and used it to improve their products. Over time, they refined the flavours and moved production from the basement kitchen to a small rented facility.Redesigning the package and calling out competitorsThe original product gained loyal customers in fitness circles, but RXBAR's biggest business breakthrough came when the founders decided to completely change its packaging. In 2015, the company dropped its original colourful labels and introduced a simple design. The front of each wrapper listed the main ingredients in large, bold letters. Below the short ingredient list, the packaging featured the words "No B.S." This message set RXBAR apart from competing protein brands that used complex medical terms to describe artificial fillers. According to the brand history published on the official RXBAR website, industry consultants initially warned Rahal and Smith that the plain design lacked traditional visual appeal and might confuse potential buyers. However, the clear and direct packaging stood out on supermarket shelves. It helped the brand attract customers beyond its original gym audience. The new packaging came with a major push into traditional retail stores. RXBAR secured distribution deals with regional grocery chains, fitness centres, and national retailers such as Target, Trader Joe's, and Whole Foods. Between 2014 and 2017, the company's annual revenue grew rapidly, rising from less than $2 million to more than $100 million.Acquiring a clean-label leaderBy 2017, RXBAR's rapid growth had caught the attention of major international food companies. These businesses wanted to benefit from growing consumer demand for healthier, less processed foods. On 6 October 2017, Kellogg Company announced a final agreement to buy Chicago Bar Company LLC for $600 million. According to official regulatory documents filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in its Form 10-Q report for the third quarter ending 30 September 2017, Kellogg paid for the purchase using a mix of short-term commercial paper and cash reserves. The SEC filing stated that RXBAR would continue to operate as an independent business unit from its Chicago headquarters. This arrangement allowed the brand to keep its company culture and flexible supply chain while gaining access to Kellogg's global distribution network. Speaking to financial analysts after the acquisition announcement, then-Kellogg CEO John Bryant described RXBAR as a unique asset that strengthened the company's position in the fast-growing market for wholesome snacks. At the time of the sale, RXBAR employed 85 full-time workers in Chicago. Its products had also expanded beyond classic protein bars to include snacks for children and plant-based protein products.Lessons from a high-speed exitThe acquisition remains one of the fastest major buyouts in the modern packaged food industry. The company went from a basement operation to a $600 million sale in just 54 months. After the acquisition, Rahal stayed on as chief executive officer for two years. He helped guide the brand as it became part of Kellogg's corporate structure before stepping down in 2019. Smith served as chief operating officer during the company's key growth years. He managed supply chain expansion and daily operations as demand increased. RXBAR's success showed how direct customer feedback and simple ingredient lists could challenge established food brands. By keeping full financial ownership and avoiding early venture capital funding, Rahal and Smith retained control of their company's shares. This allowed them to receive almost the entire financial return when Kellogg completed the buyout.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Delhi Police signals conditional nod for flag-waving, anthem at CJP's Oct 16 march amid curbs
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ march at Connaught Place on Friday, Delhi Police said it may consider
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ march at Connaught Place on Friday, Delhi Police said it may consider allowing a select group of people to gather at a suitable location to carry the national flag and sing the national anthem. The statement comes amid restrictions on gatherings in the area and the New Delhi Municipal Council’s (NDMC) decision to shut Central Park for two days.DCP PRO Neha Yadav said the CJP had appealed to the public through social media and a press conference to assemble at Central Park at 5 pm on October 16. She added that the Aam Aadmi Party had also urged its workers, supporters and the general public to attend in large numbers.“Given the current security and law-and-order situation, a prohibitory order under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) is already in effect in Connaught Place and its surrounding areas, aimed at maintaining peace and order and ensuring the safety of individuals as well as public and private property,” Yadav said.She said Delhi Police had been asked to make security arrangements at Central Park and prevent unauthorised entry. Yadav also said market and trade associations had sought protection for their establishments, alleging that unlawful gatherings were affecting business during the festive season.“The Delhi Police appeals to protesters and the general public not to participate in any gathering that violates the orders issued under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which is currently in force. Appropriate legal action will be taken against those who violate these orders,” she said.Yadav added that any permitted gathering must follow the prescribed rules for the national flag and anthem. “When carrying or accompanying the national flag, and during the singing of the national anthem, prescribed rules must be followed, and the utmost respect, dignity, and decorum must be maintained toward both the tricolour and the national anthem,” she said.NDMC shuts Central Park on October 16-17Earlier, in a notice dated October 15, the NDMC said, “It is hereby informed that the Central Park, Connaught Place, shall remain closed to the general public on 16th October 2026 & 17th October 2026, due to administrative reasons.”The closure comes after the CJP announced the march on Wednesday. On Thursday, founder Abhijit Dipke urged political parties and civil society groups to join the protest, saying, “I request all political parties and civil society groups to rise above ideology and come together. If the right to vote is not saved, democracy will not be saved.”Delhi Police tells HC it will take steps against CJP’s marchEarlier, the Delhi Police told the high court that it will take “appropriate steps” against Dipke’s proposed protest.Police also cited prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), imposed to maintain law and order and protect public and private property.The submission came as the high court heard a plea by Palika Bazar vendor Anil Kumar Gupta, who sought intervention against the proposed ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ march, arguing that protests could disrupt business and threaten traders’ livelihoods.The plea was mentioned before acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre on Thursday. Senior advocate Sacchin Puri, appearing for the petitioner, told the court, “This protest has to be stopped.”The march follows the arrest of CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were sent to five days of judicial custody after raising slogans demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation at Jantar Mantar.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Vincent van Gogh painted ‘Chestnut Trees in Blossom’ in May 1890 during his final months; after more than 60 years out of public view, it has resurfaced ahead of a New York auction with a $180 million estimate
articles.summary: Hundreds of art lovers lined up outside a Hong Kong gallery to see a Vincent van Gogh masterpiece that had been hidden from public view for more than six
articles.body: Hundreds of art lovers lined up outside a Hong Kong gallery to see a Vincent van Gogh masterpiece that had been hidden from public view for more than six decades. The 1890 painting, titled Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), reappeared ahead of a planned auction on 18 November at Sotheby’s in New York. The auction house expects the painting to sell for about $180 million (£138 million). If it reaches that price, it would set a new auction record for a work by the Dutch artist. The painting went on public display in Hong Kong as part of a worldwide preview. Large crowds came to see one of the few major late works by Van Gogh still held in private hands.Created in final weeks of lifeVincent van Gogh painted Chestnut Trees in Blossom in May 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, during the final months of his life. The landscape shows a chestnut tree covered in blossoms, with a lone man walking past three women dressed in Japanese clothing. It is one of about 70 works Van Gogh created after leaving the psychiatric asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he had painted his famous work Starry Night. Scott Niichel, a vice chairman at Sotheby's, spoke about the painting's emotional importance during a media presentation covered by Agence France-Presse (AFP). "It's one of the last, most expressive and hopeful works by van Gogh in this final phase of his career," Niichel told AFP. Van Gogh created about 70 landscapes during his short stay in Auvers-sur-Oise before his death in July 1890. Only eight of these works remain in private hands. The others are held by major museums around the world.Out of sight for six decadesThe painting has been hidden from public view for more than 60 years. According to ownership records published by Sotheby's, art collector Harriet Harris Jonas bought the painting in 1953. It was later bought through art dealer Wildenstein in 1975 by the late Argentine industrialist Carlos Pedro Blaquier and his wife, Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. The painting has remained in the Blaquier family collection ever since. It is the main work in the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection, which Sotheby's has named "Legendary." Simon Shaw, a senior adviser at Sotheby's, described the wider collection's historical importance in a statement released by the company. "What strikes me most is that the Blaquier-Arrieta collection doesn't feel like a private collection at all," Shaw said in the statement. "It feels like a small museum, a miniature Musée d'Orsay, now opening its doors for the very first time." Along with the Van Gogh landscape, the collection includes works by major Impressionist and Post-Impressionist artists such as Claude Monet, Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, and Camille Pissarro. Sotheby's expects the entire collection to raise more than $450 million when it goes up for auction in November.Testing the global art marketThe Hong Kong exhibition gave Sotheby's an important chance to measure interest among Asian collectors before the New York auction. Visitors travelled long distances to see the painting during its short stay in the city. Li Shanshan, an art lover who travelled two and a half hours from Shenzhen to view the work, shared her thoughts with the BBC. "I'd never heard of this painting before, so I wanted to see it with my own eyes," Li told the BBC. "I think it will create a huge sensation around the world." The current auction record for a Van Gogh painting is $117.2 million. The record was set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses was sold at Christie's as part of the Paul G. Allen collection. If Chestnut Trees in Blossom reaches its estimated price of $180 million, it will break that record and become one of the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction. Niichel told AFP that interest in the painting comes from around the world. He said "anything is possible" when discussing who might buy the work in November. He also said the strong public response during the Hong Kong preview suggests that a buyer from Asia is a real possibility.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Families await return of 3 Indians killed in Germany fire; Kerala CM assures help with repatriation
articles.summary: Three families in Kerala are awaiting the return of the mortal remains of their loved ones who died in a fire at a residential building in Bochum,
articles.body: Three families in Kerala are awaiting the return of the mortal remains of their loved ones who died in a fire at a residential building in Bochum, Germany, as public representatives seek the Centre’s intervention to expedite the repatriation process.The deceased were identified as Sivin Johny, 26, of Kalady in Ernakulam district, Nova Sabu, 25, of Kattappana in Idukki district, and Anjali Sheela Joy, 27, of Chemmakkad in Kollam district. The three had travelled to Germany to pursue studies or seek employment.Their families are in touch with relatives and contacts in Germany while awaiting the completion of formalities to bring the bodies back to Kerala for the last rites.CM assures all expenses for bringing bodies homeChief Minister V D Satheesan on Thursday said his office was coordinating with the Ministry of External Affairs, the Indian Embassy in Germany and Malayali associations to ensure the mortal remains were brought home at the earliest.In a post on X, Satheesan expressed grief over the deaths and conveyed his condolences to the bereaved families. He said the state government, through NORKA Roots, would bear all expenses related to repatriating the bodies.Public representatives, including MPs and MLAs, have also approached the MEA, seeking its intervention to speed up the necessary procedures.Families await return of mortal remainsLok Sabha MP Benny Behanan visited Sivin Johny’s home in Kalady on Thursday and met his parents and other relatives. In a Facebook post, he expressed grief over the deaths and said he was in touch with the German Embassy and contacts in Germany to help bring the mortal remains back.Behanan also urged the Centre and the Kerala government to expedite the formalities.Johny had travelled to Germany last month in search of employment and was expected to start a job this week, a relative told reporters. His brother, Salvin, is pursuing nursing studies in Germany.Anjali Sheela Joy had travelled to Germany in July to look for a teaching job. She was working at a warehouse while searching for opportunities in the education sector, her uncle said. Her family is now awaiting the arrangements to bring her body back.Nova Sabu had moved to Germany in July to pursue her studies and was also working part-time as a gym trainer, according to her relatives. Her father, K P Sabu, is a retired police officer, while her mother, Jyothi, works at a public health centre in Chembakappara in Idukki district.The Indian Embassy in Berlin and the Consulate General of India in Frankfurt have said they are in contact with local authorities and the bereaved families and are providing necessary assistance. German authorities are investigating the incident.For the three families, the immediate priority remains bringing their loved ones home to Kerala so they can perform the last rites.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Is Dhanush ready to make his political debut? Fan club's new avatar sparks buzz
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Actor Dhanush's official fan club has been restructured as the 'Dhanush Narpani Iyakkam' (Dhanush Welfare Movement), fuelling speculation about
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Actor Dhanush's official fan club has been restructured as the 'Dhanush Narpani Iyakkam' (Dhanush Welfare Movement), fuelling speculation about a possible political debut. The organisation unveiled a new flag and logo and announced plans to build a local network across five assembly constituencies in Coimbatore district.The restructuring was approved at an executive meeting in Coimbatore on Wednesday, news agency PTI reported. The new red-and-white flag features a large red star, with Dhanush's image at the centre.The move has drawn comparisons with actor Vijay, whose fan network evolved into a grassroots organisation before he launched the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK). TVK went on to emerge as the single-largest party in the 2026 Tamil Nadu assembly elections, winning 108 of 234 seats and forming the government with allies.Dhanush, however, has not announced any plans to enter politics.The emphasis on constituency-level organisation is a key aspect of the restructuring. The movement plans to establish local welfare units and enroll members across five assembly constituencies in Coimbatore district.Such networks can help coordinate community activities and build a sustained local presence. However, there is no confirmation that the organisation is preparing for electoral campaigning.Coimbatore could be a significant testing ground for a new political force. In the 2026 assembly elections, TVK won six of the district's 10 seats.From MGR to Vijay: The stars in politicsTamil Nadu has a long history of film stars translating screen popularity into political influence. MG Ramachandran, popularly known as MGR, founded the AIADMK in 1972 after his association with the DMK and became chief minister in 1977. His popularity helped build a political movement, backed by an organisational network and a distinct political identity.J Jayalalithaa, who followed a similar path from cinema to politics, also went on to become chief minister.Vijay is the latest major example. He made a strong electoral debut by clinching the CM chair in the first attempt itself.What has Dhanush saidThe latest restructuring follows Dhanush's appeal to supporters to move beyond film celebrations and focus on community welfare.At a blood donation camp organised by his fan clubs in Chennai in July, the actor had urged them to use their collective strength to understand local needs and help families facing difficulties.Reports have also circulated about a possible political outfit named Tamilaga Ezhuchi Kazhagam, but formal registration with the Election Commission has not been confirmed.In September, when asked about a possible political debut after receiving his National Film Awards, Dhanush laughed off the question.So, is a political debut on the cards?The new name, flag, logo and plans for local welfare units give Dhanush's fan association a more structured identity. But these steps do not, by themselves, establish that he is preparing to contest elections.A formal political announcement, a declared agenda or confirmation of party formation would provide clearer indications of his intentions. None has emerged so far.For now, the Dhanush Narpani Iyakkam could remain a welfare organisation or evolve into something larger. The political speculation is growing, but the actor has yet to signal that he is ready to make the leap from cinema to electoral politics.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Fifty arrests in organised crime probe after A66 fatal crash
articles.summary: The arrests are made as part of a wider operation against organised crime after the A66 fatal crash.
articles.body:
A total of 50 people have now been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following a fatal crash.

The arrests have been made after the head-on smash on the A66 on Teesside which killed seven people, including two police officers.

Ten of the 50 arrested are alleged to be linked to the Volvo reportedly involved in driving into two properties in the early hours of 22 August, police said.

Det Ch Sup Helen Barker of Cleveland Police, said: "Over the last two months, we have identified 50 people who we believe are associated within criminal networks that seek to cause serious violence and harm within the community through the supply of drugs."

The force said shotguns, hand guns, machetes and ammunition had also been seized, as well as £60,000 worth of class A and B drugs and more than £30,000 in cash.

Barker said: "Our pursuit of this criminality will continue, and I want to take this opportunity to thank the community for their support and patience but also for the information that we keep receiving.

"I want to encourage you to keep on reporting behaviour that is related to drugs or organised crime - no matter how small - and be assured we will act."

Safeguarding interventions have also been made in relation to three children, the force said.

On 22 August a Volkswagen Passat with five young men hit an oncoming marked Cleveland Police vehicle on the dual carriageway near Middlesbrough at about 03:39 BST.

Officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died at the scene.

The occupants of the VW Passat, which was travelling the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy - also died.

A number of those arrested have now been charged with various offences including possession of a firearm and possession with intent to supply drugs including cocaine and crack cocaine.

Fifteen people have been charged - 13 men and two women ranging in age from 19-45.
